title: Raiko and Gio: RSC at the Open Hardware Summit in Berlin
alt: Raiko and Gio presenting the Robot Study Companion at the Open Hardware Summit 2026 in Berlin
excerpt: Computer Engineering students Raiko Torga and Hiroshi Gio Kuwahara share their experiences working on the Robot Study Companion (RSC), showcasing open-source hardware at the Open Hardware Summit 2026 in Berlin, and gaining valuable insights for their Bachelor's theses.
content:
Raiko's experience

My name is Raiko Torga, and I am a Computer Engineering student. This spring, I defended my Bachelor's thesis. Four years ago, I graduated from Tartu Jaan Poska Gymnasium, where I was introduced to programming and IoT solutions. As I was interested in this field, I decided to study Computer Engineering at the University of Tartu.

During my studies at the University of Tartu, I realised that I was particularly interested in electronics design. At the Delta X Robot Basketball competition, I was responsible for the electronics in our team.

For my Bachelor's thesis, I designed a new circuit board for the Robot Study Companion (RSC). Previously, RSC relied on a specific Audio HAT board, which limited the project's long-term sustainability. The new electronics I developed support several different Audio HAT boards, making the platform more future-proof.

Robot Study Companion (RSC)

Gio's experience

My name is Hiroshi Gio Kuwahara, and I am a Bachelor's student in Computer Engineering at the University of Tartu. Before university, I studied at Tallinn Lilleküla Upper Secondary School, where I was introduced to a University of Tartu programming course called From Technology Consumer to Creator. Taking this course sparked my general interest in IT and robotics, and indirectly in computer engineering as well.

That is why I decided to study Computer Engineering at the University of Tartu.

Computer Engineering is a fairly broad field, as it involves programming, 3D modelling and electronics. By bringing these areas together, I can bring components to life, and that is what I enjoy most about the field.

My connection to the RSC project is that I am using it as preparation for my Bachelor's thesis. When I first started, I did not have any specific knowledge or ideas about RSC, but I knew that I wanted my thesis to be related to the project. Through independent projects and experimentation, I have gradually developed a clearer idea of what I would like to work on with RSC as part of my thesis, although the topic still needs to be narrowed down. In any case, I feel that the projects I have worked on so far have been both useful and valuable learning experiences. The support and inspiration of my supervisors have also been a great help.

Open Hardware Summit 2026, Berlin

On 23–24 May, the Open Hardware Summit took place in Berlin. As our thesis supervisors had attended the event before, they invited us to join them this year. We had the opportunity to see many exciting open-source hardware projects and introduce RSC to other attendees. Raiko also got to showcase the circuit board he had designed. His circuit board is open-source hardware and has received the corresponding certification, OSHWA UID EE000004.

Attending the Open Hardware Summit was particularly important to me (Gio), as I had the opportunity to meet and talk to people from different countries who share my interests in robotics and electronics. I made new connections that may prove useful in my future career. Even the opportunity to communicate in English while using technical vocabulary was a valuable and new experience for me. Explaining RSC to others also helped me deepen my own understanding of the project. Overall, the study trip was both inspiring and beneficial for my Bachelor's thesis.

The Open Hardware Summit gave us the opportunity to explore a wide range of open-source hardware projects (some of which are shown below). The programme included various talks, workshops and exhibitions related to open hardware. As Bachelor's students, we particularly valued the opportunity to attend an international event and see how our field of study connects to a wider community and real-world projects.

More than 350 people attended the event, and the two days were packed with presentations, workshops, exhibitions and other activities. What we particularly enjoyed was discovering just how diverse open hardware can be, covering everything from electronics to even footwear, which was also the subject of one of the workshops we attended.

For more information and details, visit the Open Hardware Summit exhibits page.

Some of the projects included an open-source boat, a vacuum cleaner, air quality monitoring devices, musical instruments and small robots.

Presenting RSC

In addition to the talks and workshops, the event also featured an exhibition area where our team had the opportunity to present the RSC project. This was a great opportunity to showcase what we are working on and discuss the project with people interested in robotics, open hardware and educational technology.
